problems.description: test_list_tasks_ordered_desc depends on time.sleep(0.01) between inserts and created_at ordering; if created_at is second-granularity (typical SQLite default), same-second inserts tie and the sleep does not cross a second boundary, making order non-deterministic.
ORDER BY created_at DESC assumes created_at is set with sub-second precision; ORDER BY id would be deterministic, though newest-first is the more useful behavior.

The mechanical 0.67 convention score / 16 violations (PascalCase classes, snake_case functions, UPPER_CASE constants) are pre-existing in files this commit does not touch (celery_app.py, celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py); none are introduced by this diff.

strengths: Fixes a latent SQL bug in update_task — an empty updates list would previously emit 'UPDATE tasks SET  WHERE id = ?' (invalid SQL); the early return now handles the no-op case and skips opening a DB connection.
Comprehensive pytest suite (+13 functions) covering create/read/update success paths plus edge cases (missing/blank title, 404s, empty update).
Small, focused diff (+133/-10) confined to app.py and its test file; early-return placement respects the existing get_db/dict-row pattern.
Sensible behavior improvement: tasks listed newest-first by created_at.
commit_reviews.summary: A focused, test-backed commit that fixes a latent SQL bug in update_task, improves task ordering, and adds full CRUD coverage — well-fitted to the existing Flask app; the repo-wide 0.67 convention score is a discrepancy driven by pre-existing violations in untouched celery files, not by code this commit introduces.

problems.description: JWT_SECRET falls back to a hardcoded dev value ('dev-secret-change-me...'); if the env var is unset in a real deployment, tokens are forgeable.

update_task verifies ownership via get_task(task_id, owner_id) but then executes the UPDATE filtered by id only, so ownership is checked separately from the write (TOCTOU); low impact for this single-process sqlite baseline, but a WHERE owner_id = ? clause would be safer.
migrate_db calls conn.commit() and then returns into the outer 'with get_db()' block, which commits again — redundant double commit on the migration path.
The single-file app grows by +345 lines in one session; this matches the established baseline pattern but accelerates the need for module decomposition.

The measured convention score (0.67) is driven by violations in celery_app.py/celery_config.py/celery_tasks.py — files NOT touched by this diff — plus an app.py 'Classes should use PascalCase' flag for a file that adds 0 classes; the commit's own code is convention-clean.

strengths: Per-user data isolation is done properly at the query level — every task read/write is scoped by owner_id.
Backwards-compatible schema migration (migrate_db with PRAGMA check) preserves pre-existing task data on older databases.
Mirrors existing file structure exactly: model helpers (create/get/update) and route sections follow the established single-file pattern.
Standard, well-vetted auth stack (PyJWT HS256 + werkzeug password hashing) with proper decorator hygiene via functools.wraps.
Consistent error handling and status codes (400/401/409) matching existing route conventions, plus type hints consistent with the codebase style.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, architecturally consistent feature addition that respects the baseline's single-file structure and extends it with proper per-user auth and data scoping — the low measured convention score is a repo-level artifact from untouched celery_*.py files, not this commit.

problems.description: Best-effort notification enqueue (send_notification_email.delay) runs inline in the edit_task request path; a broker outage raises and fails the primary task-update operation, coupling core CRUD availability to the notification broker. Wrap the enqueue in try/except or dispatch asynchronously.
Notification-trigger logic lives in the route handler (app.py edit_task) rather than a service layer; the edge-trigger detection is correct, but it couples the HTTP layer to the async domain concern.
The handler passes the user's username where the task parameter is named user_email — a semantic naming mismatch worth aligning in the mock payload.
edit_task now performs two DB reads (get_task then update_task) where the diff could be derived from a single read; negligible at this scale.
Minor race: previous is fetched before update_task; a concurrent delete between the reads could make previous None and raise a KeyError on previous["status"].

strengths: Clean separation of the async concern into dedicated celery_app / celery_config / celery_tasks modules with JSON serializers and a routed notifications queue
Correct edge-triggered transition detection (not-completed -> completed) rather than level-triggered re-sends, with a regression test for already-completed tasks
Thorough test coverage mocking app.send_notification_email so the suite runs without a live broker, plus a capsys test of the task itself
Respects existing patterns: type hints on public signatures, docstrings, snake_case modules, and the established pytest style in test_app.py
commit_reviews.summary: A cleanly separated, well-tested Celery notification subsystem scoring 0.85 architectural fit / 0.75 convention adherence — rated above the measured 0.67 convention score because most flagged violations are false positives from Celery-idiomatic lowercase config settings (broker_url, task_routes) that a naive PascalCase/UPPER_CASE linter misfires on, though the inline request-path .delay call does couple CRUD availability to broker health.

problems.description: find_one/find_all build column names via f-string SQL; the docstring claims safety only because keys come from code-defined dicts, but this generic pattern is easy to misuse with caller-influenced keys and broadens the attack surface versus the previous hardcoded queries.
BaseRepository inherits ABC but declares no abstract members, so the ABC is a placeholder rather than a real contract; either add abstract methods or drop the ABC.

Module-level singleton instances (task_repository, user_repository) are constructed at import time against get_db, coupling repositories to the Flask app context and complicating isolated unit testing.

Measured convention score 0.67 with 16 violations; the diff-touching app.py is flagged for a non-PascalCase class, while the majority of violations (celery_app.py, celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py) live in modules untouched by this commit and are pre-existing.

strengths: Clean repository-layer extraction removing ~98 lines of embedded SQL and duplicated DB access from route handlers in app.py
Pure refactor preserving route behavior and type hints; SonarQube shows +0 bugs and 0.0% duplication
New repositories.py code itself follows snake_case/PascalCase conventions and reuses the existing get_db idiom
commit_reviews.summary: A sound, debt-reducing repository-layer refactor that cleanly separates SQLite access from route handlers, mildly held back by a placeholder ABC and a generic f-string SQL builder that need disciplined callers.

problems.description: Breaking change: GET /tasks response shape changes from a bare JSON array to an envelope {data, next_cursor, total}; existing clients would break (all in-repo tests were updated in the same commit, so the suite stays green, but the contract change is unversioned).
Flask-Limiter is wired to Redis with swallow_errors=False, so a Redis outage would 500 every request; there is no graceful degradation path for the newly added hard runtime dependency.
count_tasks() runs a COUNT(*) over all owner rows on every page request, even when the client only needs the current page and next_cursor.
Measured cognitive complexity +16 and +1 smell attributable to this commit; list_tasks now hand-rolls cursor/limit parsing with inline try/except blocks.
Adds flask_limiter and a Redis storage backend; conftest.py fakes the server with fakeredis TcpFakeServer, which is acceptable and actually exercises the real Flask-Limiter storage code path.

strengths: Rate limiting keyed per authenticated user (JWT sub, decoded ahead of the view) with per-IP fallback is a sound design, and the rationale is documented in code.
Cursor-based pagination is implemented correctly: limit+1 has-more probe, id DESC matches insertion order, limit clamped to [1, 100], non-integer cursor/limit return 400s.
conftest.py sets RATELIMIT_STORAGE_URI before importing app, correctly avoiding the Flask-Limiter import-time race, and the autouse limiter.reset() fixture isolates tests.
Dedicated 180-line test file covering both new features; no new bugs (0), no duplication (0.0%), and existing tests were updated in the same commit to keep the suite green.
Backward-compatible repository evolution: get_tasks() gains defaulted cursor/limit parameters, and the change stays inside the existing repository pattern.
commit_reviews.summary: Solid, well-tested cross-cutting feature commit (rate limiting + cursor pagination); the measured 0.67 convention score is dominated by pre-existing violations in untouched celery_* files rather than this diff, and the main caveats are the breaking GET /tasks response envelope and the +16 complexity/+1 smell delta.
